paragraphs: I am not a doctor, but I feel the time has come to give the reader some account of Ivan’s illness. I can say one thing in advance: at that moment he was on the very eve of an attack of brain fever. His health had been poor for a long time, but it had stubbornly resisted the fever, which in the end overpowered it. I know nothing of medicine, so take this as a guess. By a terrible effort of will he had perhaps managed to put the attack off for a while, hoping, of course, to beat it altogether. He knew he was unwell. But he hated the thought of being ill at that fatal time, at the approaching crisis of his life, when he needed all his wits about him, to say what he had to say boldly and firmly and “to justify himself to himself.”

He had, however, gone to see the new doctor, the one brought from Moscow on Katerina Ivanovna’s fantastic notion, which I have mentioned already. The doctor listened to him and examined him. He decided that Ivan really did have some disorder of the brain, and he was not at all surprised by something Ivan admitted to him with reluctance. “Hallucinations are quite likely in your condition,” the doctor said, “though it would be better to check them ... You must take steps at once, without losing a moment, or things will go badly for you.” But Ivan ignored this sensible advice and did not take to his bed to be nursed. “I’m walking about, so I’m strong enough. If I drop, it will be different. Then anyone who likes can nurse me,” he decided, and that was the end of it.

And so he sat there, almost aware of his own delirium and, as I have said already, staring fixedly at something on the sofa against the opposite wall. Someone seemed to be sitting there. Goodness knows how he had got in, for he had not been in the room when Ivan came back from Smerdyakov’s. He was a man, or more exactly a Russian gentleman of a particular kind, no longer young, _qui faisait la cinquantaine_, as the French say. His dark hair was rather long and still thick, with a little gray in it, and he had a small pointed beard. He wore a brownish reefer jacket, rather shabby, though plainly cut by a good tailor. The style was at least three years old, and smart, well-to-do people had given it up two years before. His shirt and his long scarf-like necktie were the sort worn by people who want to look stylish, but a closer look showed the shirt was none too clean and the wide scarf was badly worn. The visitor’s check trousers were excellently cut, but they were too light in color and too tight for the present fashion. His soft, fluffy white hat was wrong for the season.

In short, he gave every appearance of gentility on a small income. He seemed to belong to the class of idle landowners who flourished in the days of serfdom. He had clearly moved in good, fashionable society at some time and had once had good connections, which he might even have kept. But after a gay youth he had slowly grown poor when serfdom was abolished, and he had sunk to the position of a poor relation of the best sort. He drifted from one good old friend to the next. They took him in because he was companionable and easygoing, and because he was, after all, a gentleman who could be asked to sit down with anyone, though not, of course, in the place of honor. Such obliging gentlemen in dependent positions can tell a story and make a fourth at cards, and they strongly dislike having any duties forced on them. They are usually solitary creatures, bachelors or widowers. Sometimes they have children, but the children are always being raised far away, at some aunt’s, and these gentlemen never mention the aunt in good society, as if ashamed of the connection. Little by little they lose sight of their children altogether, though now and then they get a birthday or Christmas letter from them and sometimes even answer it.

The face of the unexpected visitor was not so much good-natured as obliging, ready to put on any pleasant expression as the occasion called for it. He had no watch, but he did have a tortoise-shell lorgnette on a black ribbon. On the middle finger of his right hand was a heavy gold ring set with a cheap opal.

Ivan was angrily silent and would not start the conversation. The visitor waited. He sat exactly like a poor relation who has come down from his room to keep his host company over tea, and who stays discreetly quiet because his host is frowning and lost in thought. But he was ready for any friendly chat the moment his host began one. Suddenly his face showed concern.

“I say,” he began, turning to Ivan, “forgive me, I only mention it to remind you. You went to Smerdyakov’s to find out about Katerina Ivanovna, and you came away without learning a thing about her. You probably forgot—”

“Ah, yes,” broke from Ivan, and his face clouded with uneasiness. “Yes, I forgot ... but it doesn’t matter now, never mind, it can wait until tomorrow,” he muttered to himself. “And you,” he added, turning on his visitor, “I’d have remembered it myself in a minute, because that was exactly what was tormenting me! Why do you butt in? Do you want me to believe you put it into my head and I never remembered it on my own?”

“Then don’t believe it,” said the gentleman, with a friendly smile. “What’s the use of believing against your will? Besides, proofs don’t help belief, least of all material proofs. Thomas believed not because he saw Christ risen, but because he wanted to believe before he saw. Take the spiritualists, for example ... I’m very fond of them ... just think, they imagine they’re serving the cause of religion because the devils show them their horns from the other world. That, they say, is a material proof, so to speak, that there is another world. The other world and material proofs, whatever next! And if it comes to that, does proving there’s a devil prove there’s a God? I want to join an idealist society. I’ll lead the opposition in it. I’ll say I’m a realist but not a materialist, he he!”

“Listen,” Ivan said, suddenly getting up from the table. “I seem to be delirious ... in fact I am delirious. Talk whatever nonsense you like, I don’t care! You won’t drive me into a fury this time, the way you did before. But I feel somehow ashamed ... I want to walk about the room ... Sometimes I can’t see you and can’t even hear your voice, as happened last time, but I always guess what you’re rattling on about, because it’s _I myself speaking, not you_. The only thing is, I don’t know whether I was dreaming last time or really saw you. I’ll wet a towel and put it on my head, and maybe you’ll vanish into thin air.”
Ivan went to the corner, took a towel, and did as he had said. Then, with the wet towel on his head, he began pacing up and down the room.
“I’m so glad you treat me so familiarly,” the visitor began.

“Fool,” Ivan laughed, “you think I’d stand on ceremony with you? I’m in good spirits now, though my forehead hurts ... and the top of my head ... Only please don’t talk philosophy the way you did last time. If you can’t clear out, talk about something amusing. Tell me gossip. You’re a poor relation, so gossip is your line. What a nightmare to have! But I’m not afraid of you. I’ll get the better of you. They won’t put me in a madhouse!”

“_C’est charmant_, poor relation. Yes, I’m in my natural shape. What am I on earth, after all, but a poor relation? By the way, as I listen to you I’m rather surprised to find you’re actually starting to take me for something real, and not just a figment of your imagination, as you kept insisting last time—”

“Not for one minute have I taken you for real,” Ivan cried, in a sort of fury. “You’re a lie, you’re my illness, you’re a phantom. I just don’t know how to destroy you, and I see I’ll have to suffer for a while. You’re my hallucination. You’re myself in bodily form, but only one side of me ... of my thoughts and feelings, and only the nastiest and stupidest of them. Seen that way you might even interest me, if only I had time to waste on you—”

“Pardon me, pardon me, I’ll catch you out. When you flew at Alyosha under the lamp-post this evening and shouted at him, ‘You learned it from _him_! How do you know _he_ visits me?’ you were thinking of me. So for one brief moment you did believe I really exist,” the gentleman said with a bland laugh.
“Yes, that was a moment of weakness ... but I couldn’t believe in you. I don’t know if I was asleep or awake last time. Maybe I was only dreaming and never really saw you at all—”
“And why were you so short with Alyosha just now? He’s a dear. I behaved badly toward him over Father Zossima.”
“Don’t talk about Alyosha! How dare you, you lackey!” Ivan laughed again.
“You scold me, but you laugh, and that’s a good sign. Still, you’re ever so much more polite than you were last time, and I know why: that great resolution of yours—”
“Don’t speak of my resolution,” Ivan cried savagely.
“I understand, I understand, _c’est noble, c’est charmant_, you’re going to stand up for your brother and sacrifice yourself ... _C’est chevaleresque_.”
“Shut up, or I’ll kick you!”

“I won’t be wholly sorry, because then I’ll have got what I wanted. If you kick me, you have to believe I’m real, since nobody kicks ghosts. Joking aside, it makes no difference to me. Scold all you like, though it’s better to be a little more polite, even to me. ‘Fool, lackey!’ What words!”
“When I scold you, I’m scolding myself,” Ivan laughed again. “You’re me, myself, only with a different face. You say just what I’m thinking ... and you can’t say anything new!”
“If I think the way you do, that does me credit,” the gentleman declared, with delicacy and dignity.

“You pick out only my worst thoughts, and the stupid ones at that. You’re stupid and vulgar. You’re awfully stupid. No, I can’t stand you! What am I to do, what am I to do?” Ivan said through clenched teeth.

“My dear friend, above all I want to behave like a gentleman and be recognized as one,” the visitor began, in a burst of apologetic, simple-hearted pride, so typical of a poor relation. “I’m poor, but ... I won’t say very honest, but ... it’s an axiom accepted everywhere in society that I’m a fallen angel. I certainly can’t imagine how I ever was an angel. If I was, it was so long ago that there’s no harm in forgetting it. Now I only care about my reputation as a gentlemanly person, and I live as best I can, trying to be agreeable. I truly love men, I’ve been greatly slandered! When I stay with you here from time to time, my life takes on a kind of reality, and that’s what I like best. You see, like you, I suffer from the fantastic, so I love the realism of earth. Here, with you, everything has limits, everything is formulated and geometrical, while all we have are indeterminate equations! I wander about here dreaming. I like dreaming. Besides, on earth I turn superstitious. Please don’t laugh, that’s exactly what I like, turning superstitious. I take up all your habits here: I’ve grown fond of the public baths, would you believe it? I go and steam myself with merchants and priests. What I dream of is becoming incarnate once and for all, irrevocably, as some merchant’s wife weighing eighteen stone, and believing everything she believes. My ideal is to go to church and put up a candle in simple-hearted faith, on my word it is. Then my sufferings would be over. I like being doctored too. In the spring there was an outbreak of smallpox and I went and got vaccinated at a foundling hospital. If you only knew how I enjoyed myself that day! I gave ten roubles to the cause of the Slavs! ... But you’re not listening. Do you know, you’re not at all well this evening? I know you saw that doctor yesterday ... well, how is your health? What did the doctor say?”
“Fool!” Ivan snapped.
“Well, you’re clever, anyway. Scolding again? I didn’t ask out of sympathy. You needn’t answer. The rheumatism’s come back now—”
“Fool!” Ivan said again.
“You keep saying the same thing, but I had such a bad attack of rheumatism last year that I remember it to this day.”
“The devil have rheumatism!”
“Why shouldn’t he, if he sometimes takes on fleshly form? I take on fleshly form and I take the consequences. Satan _sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto_.”
“What, what, Satan _sum et nihil humanum_ ... that’s not bad for the devil!”
“I’m glad I’ve finally pleased you.”
“But you didn’t get that from me.” Ivan stopped suddenly, as if struck. “That never came into my head. That’s strange.”

“_C’est du nouveau, n’est-ce pas?_ This time I’ll be honest and explain it to you. Listen. In dreams, and especially in nightmares, brought on by indigestion or anything else, a man sometimes sees such artistic visions, such complex and real actuality, such events, even a whole world of events, woven into such a plot, with such unexpected details, from the loftiest matters down to the last button on a cuff, as I swear Leo Tolstoy never invented. Yet such dreams are sometimes seen not by writers but by quite ordinary people, officials, journalists, priests ... The whole matter is a complete riddle. A statesman actually confessed to me that all his best ideas came to him in his sleep. Well, it’s the same now. I may be your hallucination, but just as in a nightmare I say original things that never came into your head before. So I don’t repeat your ideas, and yet I’m only your nightmare, nothing more.”
“You’re lying. Your aim is to convince me you exist on your own and aren’t my nightmare, and now you’re saying you’re a dream.”
“My dear fellow, I’ve taken up a special method today, I’ll explain it to you later. Wait, where did I leave off? Oh, yes! I caught a cold then, only not here but over yonder.”

“Where’s yonder? Tell me, will you be here long? Can’t you go away?” Ivan exclaimed, almost in despair. He stopped pacing, sat down on the sofa, put his elbows on the table again and gripped his head tight in both hands. He pulled off the wet towel and threw it aside in annoyance. It was plainly no use.
